title: Chapter 118
content:
Xue Yang lounged by a small wooden table at a roadside stall, one leg propped up on the bench while he dug into a bowl of sweet fermented-rice soup with glutinous rice balls.

His porcelain spoon clattered merrily against the bowl. He’d been thoroughly enjoying himself until, right at the very end, he realized something unforgivable: the rice balls were plenty chewy, but the sweet broth was nowhere near sweet enough.

Xue Yang stood up and kicked the stall over.

The vendor, caught in the middle of his busywork, was struck dumb by the sudden violence.

He could only gape as the youth lashed out unprovoked, kicked the whole setup into splinters, and turned to saunter off with a smirk, not offering a single word of explanation. It took the vendor a good beat to snap back to reality before he stormed after him, spitting mad: "What the hell is your problem?!"

"Trashing your stall," Xue Yang replied casually.

Beside himself with rage, the vendor spluttered, "You're insane! You're out of your goddamn mind!"

Xue Yang didn't bat an eye. The vendor jabbed a shaking finger right in his face: "You little bastard! You eat my food without paying, and now you wreck my stall?! I ought to—"

Xue Yang’s right thumb gave a barely perceptible flick. The sword at his waist sprang from its scabbard with a crisp hiss.

Cold steel gleamed. He lightly patted the flat of Jiangzai against the man’s cheek, the gesture mocking and gentle as he drawled, sickeningly sweet: "The rice balls were great. Next time, add more sugar."

He sheathed the blade, spun on his heel, and strutted off down the street.

Paralyzed by sheer terror, the vendor swallowed his fury, staring blankly as the boy walked away. After a few paces, the knot of raw humiliation and rage finally burst in his chest.

He let out a ragged howl: "Broad daylight! Out of nowhere! What gives you the right?! What gives you the fucking right?!"

Xue Yang didn't even bother looking back. He merely gave a dismissive wave over his shoulder. "Nothing gives me the right. Plenty of things in this world happen for no reason at all. It's called bad luck. See ya!"

He strolled light-footedly past a couple of intersections. Before long, a figure caught up from behind, hands clasped behind his back, matching his pace with an unhurried, steady stride.

Jin Guangyao sighed. "The second I turn my back, you manage to drum up a mess like this. I was only supposed to cover a bowl of soup; now I have to foot the bill for the man's tables, benches, pots, and pans."

"Are you that strapped for cash?" Xue Yang asked.

"Not in the slightest."

"Then what are you sighing for?"

Jin Guangyao replied, "I would think you aren't short on coin either. Why not try playing the normal customer once in a while?"

"I never had to pay for anything I wanted back in Kuizhou," Xue Yang said. "Watch."

With practiced ease, he reached out and plucked a skewered candied hawthorn right off a passing peddler’s straw rack.

The street vendor, looking as though he’d never encountered such brazen shamelessness in his life, stood frozen with his jaw slack. Xue Yang crunched through the hard sugar shell and muttered around a mouthful: "Besides, what’s a kicked-over stall to someone like you? Can’t handle a little property damage?"

Jin Guangyao let out an amused breath. "You little hoodlum. Trash as many stalls as you want—burn down the entire avenue for all I care. Just keep one rule in mind: ditch the Sparks Amidst Snow robes, cover your face, and make sure nobody traces it back to you. Don't make my life difficult."

He tossed a handful of coins to the flabbergasted hawthorn vendor. Xue Yang spat out a hawthorn pit, his sharp eyes catching a patch of dark purple bruising clumsily concealed beneath Jin Guangyao’s temple. He burst into uproarious laughter. "What happened to your face?"

Jin Guangyao shot him a reproving sideways glance, adjusting his gauze cap to hide the contusion. "It’s a long story."

"Nie Mingjue beat you up?"

"Do you honestly think," Jin Guangyao countered smoothly, "that if he were the one who laid hands on me, I’d still be standing here chatting with you?"

Xue Yang nodded in full agreement. Fair point.

Leaving Lanling City behind, the two traversed the desolate outskirts and arrived at a bizarre, isolated compound.

There was nothing elegant about this place. Past the towering perimeter walls lay a row of grim, windowless barracks. Before the buildings sprawled an open yard cordoned off by chest-high iron bars plastered with red and yellow talismans. Inside the yard stood a collection of grotesque contraptions—heavy iron cages, crude guillotine blades, spike-boards—and a handful of ragged, shuffling "people."

These "people" bore ashen, mottled grey skin and hollow stares. They drifted aimlessly across the dirt, bumping blindly into one another while wet, rattling wheezes leaked from their slack jaws.

A corpse-refining ground.

Back then, Jin Guangshan had craved the Yin Tiger Tally so fiercely it clawed at his insides. He’d dropped countless hints and exhausted every scheme in his arsenal, but Wei Wuxian was an iron wall—immune to both carrot and stick—leaving the Sect Leader biting dust at every turn. Jin Guangshan had thought to himself: If you can forge it, why can't someone else? I refuse to believe Wei Ying is the only soul under the heavens capable of this craft. One day, someone will surpass you, trample you underfoot, and laugh in your face. Let's see how arrogant you can be then.

Driven by that obsession, Jin Guangshan lavishly recruited unorthodox practitioners who dabbled in Wei Wuxian's demonic path, dumping obscene amounts of gold and resources into them. He ordered them to reverse-engineer the Yin Tiger Tally in secret, attempting to replicate the artifact. Very few made any real headway, but the one who progressed the furthest was, astonishingly, the youngest of the lot—a street brat personally sponsored and brought in by Jin Guangyao: Xue Yang.

Overjoyed, Jin Guangshan bestowed upon him the title of Guest Cultivator, granting him sweeping authority and absolute reign. This corpse-refining ground was a secluded parcel of land Jin Guangyao had specially petitioned for him, giving Xue Yang a playground to conduct his research in complete privacy—or rather, a license to run wild without leash or consequence.

As they reached the barricades, two fierce corpses were locked in vicious combat right in the middle of the yard.

Unlike the common walking corpses, these two were dressed in intact robes, their eyes rolled back to reveal the whites. Wielding live blades, their swords clashed with a shower of shrieking sparks. Two chairs were positioned before the iron fencing. The pair sat down simultaneously; as Jin Guangyao straightened his collar, a trembling corpse shuffled over, presenting a tea bowl.

"Have some tea," Xue Yang said.

Jin Guangyao peered inside. Resting at the bottom was an eerie, swollen lump of purplish-red flesh, steeped into a bloated mess. God only knew what organ it had been carved from.

Jin Guangyao smiled, nudging the bowl back. "Thank you, no."

Xue Yang shoved it right back into his space, all sweet faux-intimacy: "This is my personal, secret recipe. Why aren't you drinking it?"

Jin Guangyao slid it back with equal warmth. "Precisely because it's your personal, secret recipe—I value my life far too much to touch it."

Xue Yang raised an eyebrow, turning his attention back to the sparring ring.

The two corpses were tearing into each other with escalating brutality, claws and blades tearing flesh until ribbons of meat flew across the dirt. Yet the boredom on Xue Yang's face only deepened. After watching for a while, he gave a crisp snap of his fingers and made a quick hand seal.

The corpses instantly convulsed. Twisting their own grips, they drew their blades across their throats and cleanly lopped off their own heads. The headless torsos crashed into the dust, twitching in violent, dying spasms.

"Weren't they fighting rather well?" Jin Guangyao asked.

"Too slow," Xue Yang muttered.

"They're considerably faster than the pair from last time."

Xue Yang raised his gloved left hand, wagging a single index finger dismissively. "Depends on what you’re comparing them to. Trash like this can't even hold a candle to Wen Ning, let alone the standard walking dead Wei Wuxian could rally with a whistle. It's downright embarrassing."

Jin Guangyao chuckled. "Why the rush? Even I'm not in a hurry. Take your time; just let me know what you need. Ah, right—"

Reaching into his sleeve, he produced an item and tossed it to Xue Yang. "Perhaps this might help?"

Xue Yang caught it and flipped through the pages. His slouched posture snapped straight. "Wei Wuxian’s manuscript?"

"The very same."

Xue Yang lowered his head, eyes burning into the ink. A moment later, he looked up. "Is this really his original handwriting? From when he was nineteen?"

"Of course. Everyone had their eye on it, clawing each other's eyes out to grab a piece. It took no small amount of effort to gather these up."

Xue Yang let out a low, appreciative curse, the feverish excitement in his eyes burning hotter. After skimming the final page, his face soured. "It's incomplete."

Jin Guangyao remarked, "Given the massive inferno and bloodbath that consumed the Burial Mounds, you should consider it a minor miracle that even these fragments survived. Savor what you have."

"What about his flute?" Xue Yang asked. "Can you get your hands on Chenqing?"

Jin Guangyao spread his hands helplessly. "Chenqing is off the table. Jiang Wanyin took it."

"Doesn't he hate Wei Wuxian's guts?" Xue Yang sneered. "What the hell does he want with the flute? Didn't you also snatch Wei Wuxian’s sword? Trade the blade for the flute. Wei Wuxian abandoned swordsmanship ages ago anyway, and Suibian is sealed tight—no one can pull an inch of steel from that scabbard. Keeping it around as a mantlepiece ornament is useless."

Jin Guangyao gave a helpless smile. "Young Master Xue really knows how to ask for the impossible. Do you think I haven't tried? Nothing is ever that simple. That Jiang Wanyin has completely lost his mind. He still refuses to believe Wei Wuxian is truly dead; he’s convinced that if Wei Wuxian ever returns, he might not bother with his sword, but he will come for Chenqing. There isn't a snowball's chance in hell he'll give it up. If I press him any further, he'll turn hostile on the spot."

Xue Yang let out a pair of mocking snorts. "Mad dog."

Right on cue, two Lanling Jin disciples dragged over a disheveled cultivator, his hair wild and tangled.

Jin Guangyao turned to Xue Yang. "Didn't you want to start a new batch of fierce corpses? Perfect timing—I brought you some raw materials."

The captive cultivator’s eyes were bloodshot, practically bulging from their sockets in blind fury. He thrashed against his bonds, his glare blazing hot enough to burn Jin Guangyao to ash. Xue Yang tilted his head. "Who's this?"

Jin Guangyao replied smoothly, his face a mask of effortless calm: "Anyone I deliver to your doorstep is, naturally, a criminal."

At those words, the captive violently lunged forward. With a mouthful of bloody spit, he managed to hack out the gag wedged in his throat: "Jin Guangyao! You treacherous, villainous beast! You dare brand me a criminal?! What crime did I commit?!"

Every syllable hit like an iron nail, spat with enough vitriol to pin Jin Guangyao to the wall. Xue Yang let out a sharp scoff. "What's the story here?"

The disciples yanked the cultivator back like a dog on a choke chain. Jin Guangyao gave a languid wave of his hand. "Gag him again."

"Wait, don't," Xue Yang cut in, leaning forward. "Let me hear it. How are you a 'treacherous, villainous beast'? He’s barking like a stray mutt, I can barely make out the punchline."

Jin Guangyao clicked his tongue with mild reproach: "Young Master He Su is considered a distinguished gentleman in refined circles. Where are your manners?"

The captive let out a bitter sneer. "I'm already at your mercy, meat on your butcher's block. Why bother keeping up the saintly facade?"

Jin Guangyao’s expression remained the picture of serene, gentle grace. "You needn't look at me like that; my hands are tied. Nominating a Chief Cultivator is simply the natural course of history. Why go out of your way to fan the flames and stir up trouble? I warned you repeatedly, yet you stubbornly refused to listen. Now that things have spiraled beyond repair, my heart truly aches with sorrow..."

He Su spat, "Natural course of history?! Stirring up trouble?! Jin Guangshan only wants to establish a Chief Cultivator so he can play at being the Wen Clan of Qishan all over again—monopolizing total power! Do you think the rest of the world is blind and deaf?! You're framing me simply because I spoke the truth!"

Jin Guangyao smiled, offering no rebuttal.

He Su snarled, "The moment your scheme comes to light, every prominent clan in the realm will see the Lanling Jin Clan for the parasites you are! You think slaughtering me will let you sleep easy at night? You're dead wrong! My Tingshan He Clan produces talent in droves! From this day forward, our entire bloodline will unite as one—we will never bend the knee to another pack of Wen dogs playing dress-up!"

At that declaration, Jin Guangyao’s eyes narrowed into delicate crescents, his lips curling into that familiar, terrifyingly pleasant smile.

Watching that expression bloom, He Su felt a cold, leaden drop in his stomach. Right then, a chaotic commotion erupted from outside the barricades, thick with the frantic weeping of women and children.

He Su whipped his head around.

A squad of Lanling Jin cultivators was dragging sixty to seventy people into the yard, all dressed in matching clan robes. Men, women, elderly, and children—all swept up in absolute terror, some wailing toward the heavens. A young girl and a teenage boy, both bound tightly with coarse rope, were shoved to their knees in the dirt.

Catching sight of him, they sobbed hysterically: "Brother!"

He Su stood paralyzed, every drop of blood draining from his face until he looked like a corpse. "Jin Guangyao! What are you doing?! If you want my life, take it! Why drag my entire family into this?!"

Jin Guangyao looked down, casually smoothing the crease of his sleeve with a mild, cheerful smile. "Did you not just remind me yourself? Killing you alone won't let me sleep easy at night. The Tingshan He Clan produces talent in droves, and from this day forward, your entire bloodline will unite as one, never bending the knee. That sounded rather terrifying. After turning it over in my head, I realized this was my only option."

It felt as though an iron fist had jammed itself straight down He Su's throat, choking out every breath. After an agonizing silence, he bellowed in raw despair: "You butcher my entire clan without cause—do you truly not fear universal condemnation?! Have you no fear of what Chifeng-zun will do when he finds out?!"

At the mention of Nie Mingjue, Jin Guangyao’s brow gave a faint twitch, while Xue Yang practically doubled over in his chair, howling with laughter.

Jin Guangyao shot him a brief glance before turning back to the prisoner, his voice sickeningly reasonable: "Come now, let's not twist words. Your Tingshan He Clan staged a treasonous uprising, rallying the entire household in a plot to assassinate Clan Leader Jin, and you were caught red-handed. How can you claim this is 'without cause'?"

From the huddled prisoners, several voices broke into hysterical cries: "Brother! He's lying! We didn't do it, we swear we didn't!"

"Absurd lies!" He Su screamed, straining against his chains. "Open your goddamn dog eyes and look at them! There are nine-year-old children in that pen! Old men who can barely walk! How could they commit treason?! Why would they target your father unprovoked?!"

Jin Guangyao replied smoothly, "Why, because you committed murder first, Young Master He Su. Naturally, your family couldn't accept your arrest."

Only then did the full horror dawn on He Su as he remembered the fabricated charge that had dragged him to this hellhole in the first place: "It's a setup! A complete lie! I never laid a finger on any cultivator from Lanling Jin! I’d never seen that dead man before in my life! Hell, who knows if he even belonged to your sect?! I... I..."

His voice caught, shattering into helpless hysterics: "I had nothing to do with it! I don't know anything! I don't know anything!"

No one in this yard was listening to his pleas. Sitting before him were two remorseless monsters who already viewed him as a slab of dead meat, taking quiet delight in watching him thrash in the dirt.

Jin Guangyao leaned back into his chair, waving a dismissive hand. "Gag him. Put it back in."

Knowing with absolute certainty that there was no way out, despair swallowed He Su whole. Gritting his teeth until they cracked, he tore his throat raw, roaring: "Jin Guangyao! Retribution will find you! Your father will rot to death in a pile of whores sooner or later, and a whore's son like you will die an even uglier death—!"

Xue Yang was grinning, soaking in the drama like cheap entertainment. Suddenly, a dark blur whipped through the air, silver light flashing in a razor-thin arc.

He Su clutched his bloody mouth, letting out a shriek of agonizing, mangled torment.
Blood splattered across the dirt. Over in the pen, He Su’s kin were coming undone—screaming, wailing, and cursing in raw panic—yet no matter how wildly they thrashed, the iron grip of their captors held fast. Standing over the crumpled, writhing form of He Su, Xue Yang casually tossed a wet, bloody strip of meat in his palm, flicking his fingers toward a pair of nearby walking corpses.

"Chuck him in the cage."

Jin Guangyao raised an eyebrow. "You’re throwing him in alive?"

Xue Yang threw him a wicked smirk over his shoulder. "Wei Wuxian never refined a live specimen. Figured I’d see what happens."

Obeying the order, the two corpses dragged He Su by his ankles, his mangled shrieks tearing through the yard, and tossed him headlong into the iron pen. Watching their elder brother violently smash his skull against the metal bars in sheer madness, a cluster of young boys and girls lunged forward against the netting, sobbing their hearts out. The shrill wails scraped like nails on stone, and Jin Guangyao pressed two fingers against his temple, massaging a creeping ache. He reached instinctively for his tea to calm his nerves, but glancing down, his gaze landed right back on the bloated, purplish lump floating at the bottom of the cup. He shifted his eyes up to the freshly severed tongue bouncing rhythmically in Xue Yang’s hand, paused for a beat, and asked, "Is that what you brewed this with?"

Xue Yang grinned. "I've got a whole jar full of 'em. Want some?"

Jin Guangyao’s face twitched faintly. "I'll pass. Clean yourself up. Come with me to fetch someone, then we can find some proper tea elsewhere."

Remembering his errand, Jin Guangyao reached up to straighten his gauze cap, inadvertently brushing the tender, purple contusion along his hairline. Xue Yang caught the wince and snickered. "Seriously, what's with all the lumps on your head?"

Jin Guangyao sighed. "I told you, it’s a long story."

Jin Guangshan spent his days dumping every shred of sect business onto Jin Guangyao while he caroused from dusk till dawn, leaving Madam Jin to blow her top back at Koi Tower on a daily basis. Back when Jin Zixuan was around, the young heir could at least play mediator between his parents; with him gone, there was nothing left to cushion the fallout. Every time Jin Guangshan went whoring, he made Jin Guangyao cover his tracks and spin flimsy excuses. Unable to get her hands on the old man, Madam Jin took out all her venom on the bastard son instead—hurling an incense burner at him one day, throwing scalding tea in his face the next. So, purely in the interest of self-preservation, Jin Guangyao had taken to personally tracking his father through the seediest corners of town, dutifully hauling him home before things escalated.

He’d done it often enough that he knew the old man's favorite haunts by heart. Tucked away in a high-end district was an opulent brothel; Jin Guangyao strode past the threshold with his hands tucked into his sleeves. The floor manager bustled over, oily smile at the ready, but Jin Guangyao waved him off with a crisp, polite flick of his hand. Behind him, Xue Yang casually swiped a fresh apple off a customer’s private table, following a pace behind as they climbed the stairs, buffing the fruit against his chest before crunching into it without a care in the world.

Before long, a chorus of shrill, flirtatious giggles drifted down from the private suites upstairs, layered over Jin Guangshan’s boisterous laughter.

"Sect Leader, look at my painting! Isn't it lovely? Stenciled right across my skin—doesn't the flower look alive?"

"What's so great about a little paint? Sect Leader, look at my calligraphy! How's my hand?"

Having rehearsed this routine a hundred times, Jin Guangyao knew precisely when to show his face and when to blend into the woodwork. He held up a flat palm, signaling for Xue Yang to halt. Xue Yang clicked his tongue, annoyance plain on his face. Just as he moved to head back downstairs to kill time, Jin Guangshan’s gruff, slurred voice bellowed from inside the room:

"A pretty girl’s job is to smell sweet, look dainty, and wear nice powder! What are you wasting ink on scrolls for? Total buzzkill."

The women had only been trying to flatter him, and the abrupt sneer knocked the wind right out of the room, leaving a sudden, awkward chill. Out in the corridor, Jin Guangyao froze, his posture stiffening for a fraction of a second.

A heartbeat later, a nervous giggle broke the hush. "Oh, but Sect Leader, didn't you hear? Back in Yunmeng, that famous courtesan had the whole world wrapped around her little finger with her poetry and prose!"

Jin Guangshan was clearly blind drunk, each syllable stumbling over his swollen tongue.

"Nonsense—sheer nonsense! I’m telling you, women are better off keeping their noses out of books. The second they read a couple of verses, they think they're cut from finer cloth than the rest. Endless nagging, wild daydreams, full of ridiculous demands—an absolute pain in the ass."

Out in the hall, Xue Yang leaned his back against the windowsill, resting an elbow on the sill as he crunched through his apple, watching the street traffic below with detached amusement. Beside him, Jin Guangyao’s smile remained plastered across his lips—delicate, curved, and completely motionless.

Inside, the courtesans chimed in with sycophantic giggles. Stumbling down some old memory lane, Jin Guangshan muttered to himself, "If I’d actually paid to buy out her contract and dragged her to Lanling, who knows how much she would’ve clawed at my robes? If she’d stayed put like a good girl, she might’ve squeezed out a few more prime years, made enough silver to see herself through. But no, she had to go and pop out a brat—a whore's son—pinning all her pathetic hopes on him..."

A girl’s sweet voice piped up. "Sect Leader Jin, who are you talking about? What son?"

Jin Guangshan waved an airy, dismissive hand. "A son? Bah, don't even mention him."

"Right, right, forget about him!"

"Since our lord isn't fond of brush and ink, we'll pack the scrolls away! Why don't we try something a little more exciting?"

Jin Guangyao stood by the banister for the burning of an incense stick, and Xue Yang watched the street below for just as long, waiting until the squeals and drunken banter upstairs finally faded into heavy, muffled breathing.

Without a word, Jin Guangyao turned around, his face a mask of placid calm, and began a slow, measured descent down the stairs. Seeing him move, Xue Yang flicked the apple core out the window and ambled down behind him.

They walked several paces in the cool night air before Xue Yang suddenly cracked, bursting into loud, merciless laughter.

"Hahahahaha! Holy shit, hahahahaha!"

Jin Guangyao stopped in his tracks, his voice icy. "What are you laughing at?"

Clutching his ribs, Xue Yang doubled over. "You should’ve seen your face in a mirror just now! That smile was so fucking fake it made me want to puke."

Jin Guangyao let out a soft sneer. "What would a little hoodlum like you understand? Fake or nauseating, a smile is a smile, and I have to wear it."

Xue Yang shrugged, completely unsympathetic. "You asked for it. If anyone called me a whore's brat, I’d hunt down his mother, fuck her raw a few hundred times, drag her out to a brothel, and let every passing degenerate have a crack at her too. Then we’d see who the real whore's son is. Simple as that."

A thin, dark chuckle escaped Jin Guangyao’s lips. "I don't share your peculiar hobbies."

"You don't, but I do!" Xue Yang shot back, grinning ear to ear. "I wouldn't mind lending a hand. Just say the word and I’ll take care of it for you, hahahaha!"

"Save your energy, Young Master Xue," Jin Guangyao replied, brushing off the offer. "Are you free in a few days?"

"Free or not, doesn't it always end up on my plate?"

"Head down to Yunmeng for me," Jin Guangyao said softly. "Clear out a certain location. Make sure it's clean."

Xue Yang smirked. "You know the saying: when Xue Yang cleans house, not even the chickens and dogs make it out alive. You worried I'll leave loose ends?"

Jin Guangyao cast him a sideways glance. "I can't say I've ever heard that saying before."

Night had fully fallen, wrapping the streets in quiet gloom as foot traffic thinned to a trickle. They ambled on, passing a small roadside vendor who was sluggishly wiping down a wooden cart. Looking up from his grease rag, the vendor took one look at Xue Yang, let out a terrified yelp, and leaped back two paces.

The man's shrill panic was so abrupt it caught Jin Guangyao off guard, his fingers instinctively brushing against the hilt of Hensheng at his hip. But recognizing a harmless stall-keeper, he dropped his hand and looked away.

Xue Yang, on the other hand, didn't waste a breath—he casually stepped up and kicked the entire cart onto its side.

Shock and outrage warred on the vendor's face. "You again?! Why?!"

Xue Yang flashed a sunny grin. "Didn't I tell you? For no reason at all."

He raised his boot for another kick, only for a sudden, searing pain to crack across the back of his hand. His pupils dilated; he whipped backward several paces on instinct. Lifting his hand, he found a cluster of angry, welted lines weeping blood across his knuckles. He snapped his head up to find a black-robed Daoist lowering a horsetail whisk, glaring at him with pure frost.

The newcomer was tall and lean, possessing sharp, severe, and utterly cold features. Clutching a whisk in one hand and bearing a long sword strapped across his back, the crimson tassel on his hilt danced lightly in the nocturnal draft. A flash of raw murderous intent flickered across Xue Yang’s eyes, and he lunged forward with an open palm strike. The Daoist flicked his whisk to parry, but Xue Yang’s footwork was slippery and erratic; twisting his angle mid-air, the palm snapped viciously toward the man's heart instead.

The Daoist’s brow knit tight. Twisting sideways to dodge, he narrowly avoided the kill-shot, though Xue Yang’s sleeve grazed his left forearm. The blow hadn't broken skin, yet a look of profound, icy disgust washed over the Daoist's face, as if brushing against vermin was more than he could bear.

Catching that fleeting look of utter revulsion, Xue Yang’s mouth twitched into a vicious sneer. Just as he moved to press the attack, a pristine blur of white stepped smoothly into the fray.

Jin Guangyao slotted himself between the two, holding out an appeasing hand. "For my sake, please stand down, Daozhang Song Zichen."

The street vendor had long since fled for his life. The dark-robed cultivator frowned. "Lianfang-zun?"

"The very same humble self."

Song Zichen’s voice remained cold. "Why does Lianfang-zun shelter such a savage delinquent?"

Jin Guangyao offered a helpless, strained smile. "Daozhang Song, this happens to be a Guest Cultivator of the Lanling Jin Clan."

"If he holds the status of a guest, why indulge in such gutter-tier barbarism?"

Clearing his throat, Jin Guangyao murmured softly, "You might not be aware, Daozhang Song... The boy has an eccentric temperament and is still quite young. Please, overlook his poor manners."

Right then, a clear, gentle voice broke through the shadows: "He is indeed quite young."

Like a sliver of cool moonlight parting the night, a white-robed Daoist carrying a horsetail whisk and a sheathed blade appeared silently at their side.

He was tall and lithe, moving with effortless grace, his flowing sleeves and sword tassel swaying like clouds trailing a breeze. Jin Guangyao offered an immediate, formal bow. "Daozhang Xiao Xingchen."

Xiao Xingchen returned the courtesy, his smile bright and unburdened. "It has been months since we last crossed paths. I am flattered Lianfang-zun still remembers me."

"Daozhang Xiao’s Shuanghua shook the cultivation world upon its drawing," Jin Guangyao replied effortlessly. "It would be stranger if I failed to remember."

Xiao Xingchen smiled, clearly accustomed to Jin Guangyao’s sugary flattery. "Lianfang-zun praises me too highly." His dark, luminous eyes drifted toward Xue Yang. "Still, young as he may be, if he holds the seat of Guest Cultivator atop Koi Tower, a measure of self-restraint is expected. The Lanling Jin Clan is an illustrious sect; it ought to set a proper example in all things."

His gaze was warm, vibrant, and entirely devoid of malice or condemnation. Even though it was a gentle reprimand, the sheer sincerity made it impossible to take offense. Jin Guangyao smoothly stepped onto the offered ladder. "Naturally."

Xue Yang let out a sharp, mocking scoff. Undisturbed by the sneer, Xiao Xingchen studied the youth for a moment, musing, "Furthermore, from the way this young man carries himself in combat, his movements are rather..."

"Vicious," Song Zichen supplied flatly.

Hearing that, Xue Yang barked a laugh. "You call me young—how much older are you two, exactly? You call me vicious—who was the prick that whipped me with a horse-hair duster the second he saw me? The pair of you lecturing people on manners is a goddamn riot."

He waved his welted, bloody hand in their faces. Clearly, he had started the scuffle by smashing an innocent man's cart, yet here he was, spinning the narrative with unshakeable audacity. Caught between a sigh and a grimace, Jin Guangyao turned to the two wanderers. "Daozhangs, this..."

Xiao Xingchen couldn't help a faint, amused smile. "You truly are..."

Xue Yang’s eyes narrowed into slits. "Truly what? Go on, spit it out."

"Chengmei, that’s enough," Jin Guangyao chided gently.

The moment that courtesy name crossed his lips, Xue Yang’s face darkened dangerously.

Jin Guangyao turned back to the Daoists with a placating bow. "My apologies for tonight's unpleasantness. For my sake, please do not hold it against him."

Song Zichen simply shook his head. Xiao Xingchen reached out, patting his friend's shoulder. "Zichen, let us go."

Song Zichen met his eyes, gave a small nod, and the two offered Jin Guangyao a parting bow before stepping into the darkness side by side.

Xue Yang stared after their receding figures, a venomous smile pulling across his clenched teeth. "...Fucking stinking Daoists."

Jin Guangyao raised an eyebrow. "They barely touched you. What warrants such deep resentment?"

"I despise high-and-mighty hypocrites who think their shit doesn't stink," Xue Yang spat. "That Xiao Xingchen is barely older than me, yet he acts like the world’s self-appointed hall monitor. Makes my skin crawl, preaching at me like that. And that Song prick..." His lips peeled back in a savage grin. "I barely brushed his arm, and he looked at me like I was filth. Mark my words—one day, I'll scoop his eyes out, crush his heart to paste, and see how arrogant he looks then."

Jin Guangyao clicked his tongue. "You're misreading him. Daozhang Song simply has an aversion to filth and dislikes physical contact with anyone; it wasn't personal."

"Who are those two, anyway?"

"You've been causing trouble for so long, and you don't even know who they are?" Jin Guangyao asked, mildly amused. "They're the talk of the realm right now: Xiao Xingchen of the bright moon and gentle breeze; Song Zichen of the proud snow and frosted pines. Never heard of them?"

"Never heard of 'em, don't care," Xue Yang scoffed. "A couple of nobodies."

"Heard of them or not, it matters little," Jin Guangyao replied. "The point is, they are men of virtue. Just leave them alone."

"Why?"

Jin Guangyao smiled faintly. "As the saying goes: Better to offend a scoundrel than to cross a righteous man."

Xue Yang gave him a deeply skeptical look. "Is that how the proverb goes?"

"Naturally. Cross a scoundrel, and you can simply slit his throat to end the trouble; onlookers might even applaud your handiwork. Cross a righteous man, however, and you'll find yourself tangled in a nightmare. Those types are relentless, hounding your heels to the ends of the earth, and if you so much as graze them, the entire world will scream for your head. It’s best to keep your distance. Tonight, we were lucky they wrote you off as a hot-headed brat throwing a tantrum. If they knew what you actually spent your days doing, they would never let you off the hook."

Xue Yang snorted with boundless contempt. "Tied up in your own rules. I'm not scared of that righteous garbage."

"You might not be, but I am," Jin Guangyao murmured smoothly. "Fewer headaches make for a longer life. Come on."

A few steps later, they arrived at a fork in the road. To the right lay the gilded ascent to Koi Tower; to the left, the dark trail leading down to the corpse-refining grounds.

Trading a brief, knowing smile, the two parted ways into the night.
